kp.k: Harvey Moot customizes AI for Supreme Court preparation
kp.d: In this May 7, 2026 company blog, Harvey's authors report that Neal Katyal approached the company the previous year about assisting his team's case preparation. Harvey assembled lawyers and AI researchers to develop a custom version called Harvey Moot. The account presents a specific deployment for experienced litigators rather than a measured study of effectiveness.
qs: Neal reached out to us last year to ask about how Harvey might be able to help his team prepare for cases.
A small team of dedicated lawyers and AI researchers worked with Neal’s team to create a custom version of Harvey we now call Harvey Moot.

kp.k: AI supplements advocacy through simulated questioning and response preparation
kp.d: The authors report that Katyal was initially skeptical but found Harvey useful as a sparring partner for anticipating Justices' questions and considering persuasive responses. They relay his description of the tool as his team's “peripheral vision” and argue that AI can refine preparation while allowing lawyers to spend more time on judgment and strategy. This is an augmentation claim, not a claim that AI replaces the advocate.
qs: He is the first to admit that he was initially skeptical of how AI could augment his proven, successful methodology to prepare for the most high profile cases.

But what he and his team saw was notable: the opportunity for Harvey to be a sparring partner, anticipating not just the likely questions and responses from the Justices, but also how he might consider responding in a manner that resonates.
In his TED Talk, Neal calls Harvey his team’s “peripheral vision.”
What he experienced at the highest level is true for all of us: AI can help sharpen our approach, refine our preparation, and ultimately, spend more time on judgment and strategy.

kp.k: Reported litigation uses illustrate adoption rather than quantified outcomes
kp.d: The authors report Harvey Moot's use in Katyal's preparation for the Tariffs case and describe Harvey's contribution as a small part of the team's preparation. They also identify Matt Nelson of Warner Norcross + Judd as using Harvey when arguing Pung vs. Isabella County. These are reported practitioner examples; the document supplies no comparative performance results or quantified contribution to litigation outcomes.
qs: We were honored to be a small part of their intense preparation, but what we are most proud of is the potential this work creates for our academic partnerships and for future case preparation.
Neal is not the only lawyer who has leveraged Harvey to prepare for a case before the Supreme Court.

[Matt Nelson of Warner Norcross + Judd](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/warner-norcross-judd-llp_warner-partner-matt-nelson-prepares-for-scotus-activity-7431785241725399041-tZGh/) used Harvey when he argued Pung vs. Isabella County.

kp.k: Law school rollout targets experiential advocacy training
kp.d: Harvey says it is starting with law school partners to bring Harvey Moot into classrooms, enabling students to workshop real-life examples with the tool used by Katyal's team. The authors frame this as a prospective change in teaching methods and intend to use student feedback to adapt the model for other courts and legal systems, including real-time argument practice with Justice-specific inputs.
qs: To make that a reality, we are starting with our law school partners to bring Harvey Moot to the classroom, giving students the chance to workshop real life examples with the same tool Neal and his team used.
In so doing, the goal is give students and faculty members alike a unique opportunity to bring a new teaching approach to something that has largely been instructed the same way for decades.

We’ll use the feedback from law students to replicate this model with courts, law schools, and lawyers around the world, and in so doing will move from reading and writing draft arguments to practicing them in real time with highly instrumented inputs on each specific Justice.

kp.k: Access-to-justice ambition rests on broader access to preparation tools
kp.d: The authors connect wider availability of elite advocacy preparation tools with Harvey's stated access-to-justice mission and with renewed emphasis on debate, storytelling and reasoning. This is an aspirational argument about expanding opportunities; the document does not report outcomes concerning unmet civil legal need.
qs: We have said from the early beginnings of Harvey that our ultimate goal is to increase access to justice and to transform how the legal field works.

By democratizing access to a tool that one of the world’s leading appellate attorneys used to refine his team’s arguments in a landmark victory, our goal as a company is to create more opportunities to take the practice of law back to its roots in debate, storytelling, and reasoning.
Access to justice begins when you increase the aperture of what’s possible and who it’s possible for, and this project is one more meaningful step in advancing that objective for our team at Harvey.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors present Harvey Moot as an AI sparring partner that augments advocacy preparation, and propose extending it into legal education and other court systems.
pts.d: Winston Weinberg, Gabe Pereyra and Julio Pereyra claim that Harvey can help lawyers anticipate judicial questions and responses, refine their own responses, and devote more time to judgment and strategy. They describe augmentation of experienced lawyers rather than replacement or autonomous advocacy. They also propose using Harvey Moot in law-school classrooms to let students workshop real-life examples with the tool used by an experienced Supreme Court team. Their longer-term ambition is to extend the model internationally and move beyond drafting arguments toward real-time practice informed by justice-specific inputs. They frame wider access to the preparation tool as a contribution to access to justice, but do not report a measured reduction in unmet civil legal need.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of company-reported practitioner use, custom development experience and a referenced practitioner account, rather than quantitative testing.
pts.d: The authors describe a small team of Harvey lawyers and AI researchers developing a custom tool with Neal Katyal’s team. They cite Katyal’s Supreme Court experience and his TED Talk about using Harvey Moot during preparation for the Tariffs case, which they describe as a landmark victory. They report his initial skepticism and subsequent experience, including his description of Harvey as his team’s “peripheral vision.” They also identify Matt Nelson’s use of Harvey in Pung vs. Isabella County; the text does not specifically identify his tool as Harvey Moot. These are reported use cases and experiential support. The document provides no controlled comparison, benchmark, quantified time savings or measured educational outcomes, and does not establish that Harvey caused the litigation victory. Educational and international benefits are presented as goals to be developed with future student feedback.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes completed Supreme Court preparation from an emerging classroom rollout and an undated international expansion.
pts.d: Writing on May 7, 2026, the authors say Katyal approached Harvey “last year,” implying 2025, and describe a TED Talk launching during the publication week about preparation already undertaken. The courtroom preparation claims concern a custom version developed collaboratively with Katyal’s team. Classroom deployment is described as starting with existing law-school partners. Replication for other courts and legal systems is a future plan informed by student feedback, with no completion date, availability terms or scale specified. Broader claims about improving preparation and freeing time for judgment are expressed as capabilities, not quantified guarantees.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Immediate users are appellate lawyers and their teams; proposed beneficiaries include law students, faculty and lawyers in other jurisdictions.
pts.d: For experienced Supreme Court advocates, the claimed benefit is stronger preparation through simulated questioning and response refinement, while lawyers retain judgment and strategy. For students, the proposed benefit is access to an elite advocate’s preparation tool and opportunities to practice realistic arguments. Faculty are offered a new teaching approach, and students are also expected to provide feedback for product adaptation. Courts, law schools and lawyers worldwide are prospective participants in expansion. The public is an implied beneficiary of the company’s access-to-justice ambition, but the source does not specify underserved populations, affordability arrangements or a direct service-delivery mechanism addressing unmet legal need.
